capturedCatalogNamespace.graph_drag_model_note: This flight includes air drag. The drag force depends on total speed, coupling horizontal and vertical motion. Gravity stays constant; total acceleration changes.
capturedCatalogNamespace.graph_vacuum_model_note: This flight has no air drag. Horizontal and vertical motion are independent; gravity changes only vertical velocity.
capturedCatalogNamespace.concept_projectile_models: Without air drag, the path is a parabola: horizontal velocity stays constant while gravity changes vertical velocity. With drag, both components change and the path is asymmetric.
capturedCatalogNamespace.concept_energy_models: Without air drag, kinetic energy (½mv²) and gravitational potential energy (mgh) exchange while their sum stays constant. Drag transfers mechanical energy to the surroundings, so KE + PE decreases.
capturedCatalogNamespace.concept_gravity_vacuum: With air drag off and the same launch speed and angle, Moon gravity (1.6 m/s²) gives about 6 times the range of Earth gravity (9.8 m/s²).
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth1_models: With air drag off, no horizontal force is needed to keep horizontal velocity constant. The horizontal arrow shows velocity. With air drag on, a backward drag force slows that motion.
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth_model_assumptions: Unless a question explicitly includes air resistance, assume no air drag. Range comparisons use equal launch and landing heights and hold the other launch settings constant.
capturedCatalogNamespace.iq_ideal_intro: This calculator assumes no air drag and equal launch and landing heights. Its sliders are separate from the flight controls. Range changes with speed and gravity; the rating compares your angle with 45° at the same speed and gravity, so only angle changes the rating. Apply these settings to test the prediction in the simulator.

capturedCatalogNamespace.concept_projectile_body: An object launched into the air follows a parabolic path. Horizontal velocity (Vx) stays constant while vertical velocity (Vy) changes due to gravity. Enable Vectors to see!
capturedCatalogNamespace.concept_newton2_body: F = ma. The only force on a projectile (ignoring drag) is gravity: a = g downward. This creates the curved trajectory.
capturedCatalogNamespace.concept_optimal_body: Without air resistance, 45° gives maximum range. With drag, the optimal angle shifts lower (~38-42°). Try it!
capturedCatalogNamespace.concept_energy_body: Kinetic Energy (KE = ½mv²) converts to Potential Energy (PE = mgh) and back. Enable the Energy bar to watch this live!
capturedCatalogNamespace.concept_air_body: Drag force opposes motion and increases with speed (F_drag ∝ v²). It shortens range, lowers max height, and makes the trajectory asymmetric.
capturedCatalogNamespace.concept_gravity_body: Different planets have different gravitational pull. Moon (1.6 m/s²) lets projectiles fly 6x farther than Earth (9.8 m/s²)! Try Jupiter for a challenge.
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth1_label: Myth: “A moving object needs a forward push.”
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth1_body: Watch Vx — it never changes, and the Vectors view shows NO horizontal arrow. With no sideways force, the object keeps moving sideways on its own (Newton's 1st Law).
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth2_body: Drag the Mass slider — the trajectory does NOT change. In a vacuum every mass falls with the same g; mass only scales the energy bar, never the path.
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth3_label: Myth: “Velocity points where the force points.”
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth3_body: At the very top of the arc the velocity is purely horizontal, yet gravity still points straight DOWN. A force changes motion — it doesn't have to point along it.

capturedCatalogNamespace.air_drag_modifies: Air drag modifies these equations — real range will be shorter than the idealized calculation below.
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth35_1_s: A heavier cannonball falls faster, so it lands sooner.
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth35_1_why: Gravity speeds up EVERY mass equally (with air resistance off) — a 10 kg ball and a 1 kg ball trace the exact same arc. Galileo’s big idea.
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth35_1_tryit: Launch with mass = 1 kg, then slide mass to 10 kg and launch again. Same arc, same landing spot.
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth35_2_s: At the very top of the arc, the ball has stopped moving.
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth35_2_why: Only the UP-DOWN part of the motion pauses at the top. The ball keeps moving forward the whole time.
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth35_2_tryit: Turn on Vectors and watch the horizontal arrow at the top of the arc — it never shrinks.
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth35_3_s: Doubling the launch speed doubles the distance.
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth35_3_why: Distance grows with speed × speed. Double the speed and it lands FOUR times farther.
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth35_3_tryit: Launch at 15 m/s, then at 30 m/s with the same angle — compare the landing markers.
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth35_4_s: Aiming at 45° throws the farthest (no air).
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth35_4_why: Lower angles fly flat but fall too soon; higher angles waste speed going up. 45° is the perfect trade.
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth35_4_tryit: Run the complementary-angles demo — 30° and 60° even land on the SAME spot.
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth68_1_s: After launch, a force keeps pushing the ball forward.
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth68_1_why: Once it leaves the cannon, the ONLY force is gravity, pulling straight down. Forward motion continues because nothing stops it — Newton’s first law.
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth68_1_tryit: Watch the vector overlay in flight: there is no forward force, yet Vx stays perfectly constant.
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth68_2_s: A ball fired horizontally and a ball dropped from the same height hit the ground at the same time.
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth68_2_why: Horizontal and vertical motion are independent. Both balls fall with the same gravity from the same height, so they land together.
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth68_2_tryit: Fire at a very low angle and compare the flight time with a steep, short lob from the same height.
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth912_1_s: With air resistance ON, 45° is still the best angle.
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth912_1_why: Drag punishes long, high flights — it bleeds v² the whole way. The optimum drops to roughly 30–40° depending on speed.
capturedCatalogNamespace.myth912_1_tryit: Toggle air resistance on and sweep the angle slider — watch where the landing marker actually peaks.
capturedCatalogNamespace.iq_intro: Three sliders control gravity (any planet), launch angle, and velocity. The simulator tells you whether your projectile range is near-optimal, reasonable, or far-off — a discrete 3-state outcome (no numeric score). Sweep the sliders. Log observations. Type what you discover.

capturedCatalogNamespace.a11y_canvas_desc: Physics projectile simulator canvas. Cannon on left fires projectiles across a landscape with target flags at 50m, 100m, 200m, 300m. Shows trajectory trail, velocity vectors, and impact particles.

capturedCatalogNamespace.next_try_drag: Turn on Air Drag and launch again: the dashed ghost is the no-drag path, and the Last flight strip shows what drag cost.

capturedCatalogNamespace.toast_45_own_complement: 45° is its own complement! Try 30° or 60° to see the symmetry.
capturedCatalogNamespace.toast_complementary: are complementary (sum to 90°) so they land at the same spot (without drag).
capturedCatalogNamespace.est_section_blurb: Closeness earns estimation XP here because numerical calibration is the skill. Your reflection earns completion credit regardless of the error.

capturedCatalogNamespace.runlog_caption: Experiment log: launch settings, measured range, and which variable changed between runs
capturedCatalogNamespace.runlog_confounded: more than one change, so the result cannot be pinned on any single variable
capturedCatalogNamespace.runlog_fair_count: of your comparisons changed exactly one variable. Those are the ones you can draw a conclusion from.

capturedCatalogNamespace.quiz_world_moon: Moon gravity is ~6× weaker than Earth’s, so everything flies ~6× farther.
